title: David Byrne’s New Book Explores the Strange Afterlife of Good Ideas: From Vermeer’s Paintings to Roman Concrete & Dark Matter

David Byrne will always be most wide­ly known as the co-founder
body:
in Art, Books, History, Technology |   	October 9th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

David Byrne will always be most wide­ly known as the co-founder and front­man of Talk­ing Heads. That may count among the great­est pos­si­ble achieve­ments for any artist — to the minds of many an Open Cul­ture read­er, at least — but it must occa­sion­al­ly frus­trate the man him­self. Talk­ing Heads broke up 35 years ago, but Byrne has only grown more and more pro­duc­tive since, record­ing his own albums, cre­at­ing musi­cals, writ­ing books, putting on Pow­er­Point pre­sen­ta­tions, and even design­ing bike racks. By now, his ideas have stretched so far beyond music that he’s con­sid­er­ing the nature of ideas them­selves, how they suc­ceed or fail in catch­ing on, and why they go in and out of accep­tance over time. Hence his new book Sleep­ing Beau­ties: Why Good Ideas Go Dor­mant and How They Wake Up.
“I first saw the term ‘sleep­ing beau­ties’ (out­side of the folk­tale or the Dis­ney movie) when I went down a rab­bit hole and stum­bled on a paper from 2004 called “Sleep­ing Beau­ties in Sci­ence” by the sci­en­to­met­rics researcher Antho­ny van Raan at Lei­den Uni­ver­si­ty,” Byrne writes in an excerpt of the book pub­lished online. (Sci­en­to­met­rics being, he adds, “the study of the impact and com­mu­ni­ca­tion of sci­ence.”) He cites a favorite exam­ple of the astronomer Vera Rubin’s dis­cov­ery, in the nine­teen-sev­en­ties, of “evi­dence for dark mat­ter, which is esti­mat­ed to make up a large percent­age of the uni­verse.” Under­stand­ing her own obser­va­tions required her to “ques­tion even her most basic assump­tions — that mat­ter must emit light and radi­a­tion. She was a visu­al thinker, and she used her data to cre­ate plots and sketch­es that revealed pat­terns with­in the num­bers.”
Only decades lat­er was Rubin’s coun­ter­in­tu­itive vision of the uni­verse sup­port­ed by the­o­ret­i­cal physi­cists and radio astrono­mers using ever more tech­no­log­i­cal­ly advanced tools like “the pow­er­ful Hale Tele­scope, Kent Ford’s new spec­tro­graph, and the Uhu­ru satel­lite, which tracked cos­mic X‑rays.” In the Sci­ence Fri­day inter­view at the top of the post, Byrne brings up a much old­er, longer-sleep­ing beau­ty often fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture: ancient Roman con­crete, the source of whose extra­or­di­nary strength and endurance was only deter­mined a few years ago. Though espe­cial­ly vivid in tech­nol­o­gy and sci­ence, “this for­get­ting and then remem­ber­ing, I knew from my own expe­ri­ence, wasn’t lim­it­ed to acad­e­mia,” he writes. “It hap­pens in all kinds of fields and endeav­ors — music, art, lit­er­a­ture, every kind of cre­ative pro­fes­sion.”


	

As Adam Grant writes in the New York Times Book Review, the range of exam­ples cov­ered in Sleep­ing Beau­ties includes “how advo­cates reawak­ened Bach’s com­po­si­tions and Ver­meer’s paint­ings after one and two cen­turies of slum­ber; how tech­no­log­i­cal advances rekin­dled the­o­ries of con­ti­nen­tal drift and black holes; how acci­dents resus­ci­tat­ed hand-wash­ing and genet­ics; and how war renewed inter­est in the sub­ma­rine and The Great Gats­by.” Mak­ing an appear­ance on Late Night with Seth Mey­ers, Byrne was asked if any of his own work has under­gone a sim­i­lar process of dis­in­ter­est fol­lowed by redis­cov­ery. “It’s kind of the oppo­site,” he replies. “There’s things that I’ve done where I go, ‘That one does not hold up that well at all’ ” — which, if the irony of cul­tur­al his­to­ry con­tin­ues to oper­ate as usu­al, will be exact­ly the records the chil­dren of today’s Talk­ing Heads fans put on most enthu­si­as­ti­cal­ly a few years down the line.
Relat­ed Con­tent:

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Jonathan Knight's Meditative Series 'Exhale' Invites Us to Slow Down and Practice Noticing
description: “A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention,” economist and computer scientist Herbert Simon warned in 1971. In our era of digital ove
body:
“A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention,” economist and computer scientist Herbert Simon warned in 1971. In our era of digital overload, it feels increasingly urgent—ironically—to remember to slow down. Too often we’re distracted by one thing or the next, looking down at our screens or paying attention to our surroundings just briefly enough to snap a photo before moving on. Jonathan Knight is captivated instead by the quiet moments, the beauty in stillness, and the gentle, gradual changes around us that take time to fully appreciate.
Known for his ethereal, minimalist images, Knight conceived of Exhale as a way to explore the nuances of color and “the emotional experience of looking,” he says in a statement. On one hand, the photos are of water, but it may be more apt to describe them as portraits of atmosphere. Clear skies brimming with stars complement foggy mornings and a billowing release of rain from a heavy cloud. 

“The project grew out of my background in both photojournalism and landscape architecture, and from thinking about how we experience landscapes differently when we stop trying to document them and simply spend time with them,” Knight says. He adds:

There is also a technological tension at the heart of the work. We now live in a culture of instantaneous image-making, computational photography, AI-generated imagery, and endless visual consumption. Yet I’m deliberately using technology to do almost the opposite: to slow the photographic process down and make images that resist immediate consumption.

There is a sense of restraint in these images, where a lack of “flashiness” and few defining events lend a sense of the mundane. This is an invitation: through long exposure, both photographically and in the act of looking itself, Exhale invites us to practice noticing.
See more on Knight’s Instagram.

title: Symmetry Meets the Sacred in Shuling Guo's Dreamy, Diffused Paintings
description: “I left my hometown / My hometown appears,” begins a poem by artist Shuling Guo titled “Temple II,” which shares its name with her forthcoming sol
body:
“I left my hometown / My hometown appears,” begins a poem by artist Shuling Guo titled “Temple II,” which shares its name with her forthcoming solo exhibition at Hollis Taggart Downtown. Drawing on sacred symbolism and nature, Guo delves into her memories of growing up in Chaoshan, Guangdong Province, China, and the area’s unique mixture of spiritual and folk traditions. Her dreamlike, symmetrical works speak to the harmony of the cosmos as much as they nod to the balance of life and the sublime.
Guo’s paintings in Temple II explore memory, presence, and loss, and their creation coincided with both the birth of her daughter and the death of her grandmother. Burgeoning blossoms, delicate flames, and glowing ribbon-like tendrils allude to the transience of life, its beauty, and its fragility.
“Purple Glow” (2026), oil and colored pencil on linen over panel, 20 x 16 inches
The artist views the body as a temple, including the mind, which links one’s physical experience to the psychological and emotional. Guo is influenced by her earliest interactions with ceremony and ritual in Guangdong Province, where locals practice Daoist and Buddhist traditions alongside folk customs. “Guo made frequent visits to her village temple, where local wood carving, murals, and sculpture became part of her visual memory,” the gallery says.
Religious imagery, especially from the Early Renaissance, informs Guo’s compositions, especially with the addition of arch-like features within which flowers droop or birds perch. The combination of oil paint and colored pencil creates diffused, otherworldly forms that also evoke the effervescent spiritualist paintings of Agnes Pelton, and orchids and other flowers suggest sensuality and human anatomy not unlike Georgia O’Keeffe. In Guo’s works, “these different visual traditions converge as a way of exploring devotion and ritual,” the gallery says.
Temple II opens on October 15 and continues through December 5 at Hollis Taggart Downtown, 109 Norfolk Street, New York. The show will also feature the artist’s first mural, which transforms the gallery into an immersive, meditative space. See more of the artist’s work on Instagram.

title: New Art Books from the Quarto Group
description:
Announcement
                From art history to instruction, Quarto publishes visually-rich books for artists of all mediums and ski
body:
Announcement
                From art history to instruction, Quarto publishes visually-rich books for artists of all mediums and skill levels.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            Quarto publishes visually-rich books for artists of all mediums and skill levels. Explore highlights from the 2026 collection!Light & Color in the Watercolor LandscapeBy Vladislav YeliseyevDiscover the secrets to capturing depth, atmosphere, and emotion in your watercolor landscapes with Light and Color in the Watercolor Landscape. Acclaimed artist and instructor Vladislav Yeliseyev shares his proven techniques for harnessing light and shadow, creating luminous colors, and refining compositions to enhance realism and impact.Frida Kahlo at HomeBy Suzanne BarbezatDiscover the intimate spaces that shaped one of the world’s most iconic artists. This compelling visual biography traces Kahlo’s life through the places she loved, from her childhood in Coyoacán and her student years in Mexico City, to her time in the United States, and her final return to La Casa Azul. Drawing on archival photographs, family images, personal artefacts, and Frida’s own paintings, the book uncovers how home was not merely a backdrop but a central force in her art and self‑expression.New Lessons in Landscape PaintingBy Mitchell AlbalaRefine and expand your landscape painting skills with this next-level guide by award-winning painter and bestselling author Mitchell Albala. New Lessons in Landscape Painting builds on the success of the bestselling The Landscape Painter’s Workbook, with new topics, step-by-step exercises, demonstrations, and in-depth painting analyses. Each is designed to build stronger skills in the core practices of landscape painting: shape interpretation, composition, and color.The Wild Magic of IcelandBy Norris NimanFor centuries, the breathtaking waterfalls, fierce volcanoes, and sweeping green hills of Iceland have captivated travelers’ imaginations. In The Wild Magic of Iceland, acclaimed photographer and adventurer Norris Niman transports you to these and more picturesque sites on a visual adventure through the seasons, featuring 100+ dazzling photographs.Paul Nicklen: A Photography MasterclassBy Paul NicklenJoin Paul Nicklen – renowned conservationist, wildlife and art photographer – for a rare, tell-all masterclass in photography. Drawing on more than three decades of experience, including 20 years of shooting for National Geographic, Nicklen distils his craft into 20 key lessons, each with a clear and simple takeaway.Art of the New York SubwayBy Adrian BruneStep into the world’s largest underground art museum with Art of the New York Subway, a stunning tribute to the artistry that transforms the New York subway from a transit system into a cultural landmark. Tracing nearly 200 stations of the subway, this book celebrates the fusion of architecture, design and public art that defines New York’s identity.Wanderlust InkBy Ollie SmitherWanderlust Ink is a stunning collection of fine-line tattoo designs that amaze and inspire. These thoughtful, hand-drawn designs by popular artist and designer Ollie Smither (@os.illustration) demonstrate a passion for travel, adventure, nature, and connectivity of all kinds.The Art of the UnknownBy S. ElizabethThe Art of the Unknown is an enthralling journey for anyone fascinated by mystery and the esoteric, inviting you to look again at the forces that persist just beyond the threshold of ordinary reality, and to discover how artists have long attempted to make the invisible visible.Learn more at quarto.com

title: Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land
description:
Interview
                The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist talks about his recent performances at the Park Avenue Armory,
body:
Interview
                The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist talks about his recent performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the freedom of improvisation, and the privilege of “deep listening.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Diné (Navajo) composer, performer, and visual artist Raven Chacon performs in the Veterans Room as part of Park Avenue Armory’s 2026 Artists Studio series on Wednesday, October 7. (all photos Da Ping Luo, courtesy Park Avenue Armory)
    
        
            On Wednesday and Thursday night, sound mixers, synthesizers, pedals, speakers, whistles, a turkey call, and a ceramic horn sat on a table at the center of the Veterans Room in Manhattan’s Park Avenue Armory. Serving as the stage for Raven Chacon’s hour-long improvisation sessions for the Armory’s Artists Studio series, the table also offered audiences the rare opportunity to see the prolific artist at play.During his performance on October 8, the Diné artist, composer, and Pulitzer Prize-winner used each object on the table to surprising and often discomfiting ends. He rigorously blew a whistle into a microphone, looping the sound and layering it atop a rising drone, which he intermittently cut to make room for the electronic transmission of the breath he recorded moments earlier. He mixed screeches over the whistles, eventually transforming the former into an oscillating, metallic sound redolent of the extraterrestrial signals in a sci-fi film. When the composition strayed too far into speculative abstraction, he’d snap it back with a clear, often frightening reminder of the world outside. Chacon ended the session by playing recordings of the wind through a hyperdirectional speaker that he moved in a circle around himself. He swept the sound of the wind over a new part of the room with each turn, transmitting with it the geography of alternative worlds much less violent than those sounded by the cars blaring up and down Park Avenue immediately outside, but whose continued existence depends upon our choosing to listen.I talked with Chacon over the phone between his performances at the Armory about the role of location in his work, his repurposing of tools associated with colonial violence, and his turn to science fiction for an upcoming show at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. Hyperallergic: For your Arts and Letters show, you were working with both local naturalist histories and the Lenape culture and history of New York. How do you bring site-specificity to a work like this that's entirely improvised?Raven Chacon: I wish I could say I was responding to the Armory [laughs]. When I’m playing in the city, I tend to bring in more field recordings of the outdoors, of wind and other sounds from other places. A lot of these were gathered where I'm from in New Mexico. While not site-specific to the Armory in this case, I find myself incorporating those more indoors, amongst the other things that encroach upon the interior of the space. It’s unavoidable that we might hear sirens and traffic outside, and those usually become part of the soundtrack of what I’m working with.H: Those sounds can have a different effect just based on the setting. We recently published a review of a group show you were in at the Hammer that likens your sound piece to a “California earthquake,” which is the type of resonance that you wouldn't get in New York.RC: That was certainly a consideration. Also, with that show, there were a lot of works about the actual ground. That installation was situated at the entry, but immediately, you have works by Edgar Calel, Ana Mendieta, these works that involve soil and dirt. I wanted to reference that with that piece. And as you move through, you have these different interactions with different materials and visual concepts happening throughout the show.Chacon working with synthesizers, mixers, and pedals during the session

title: Gochman Collection of Indigenous Art to Open Katonah Space in November
description:
News
                The new home in New York, known as Branchline, will display selections from the family’s trove of over 800
body:
News
                The new home in New York, known as Branchline, will display selections from the family’s trove of over 800 contemporary Native artworks.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            From left to right: Rachel Martin, Becky Gochman, Audrey Lea Collins, Nicole van Brugge, Moonoka Begay, and Laura Phipps, of the Gochman Family Collection team (photo Denis Gutierrez-Ogrinc, courtesy Gochman Family Collection)
    
        
            Branchline, a permanent exhibition space for the Gochman Family Collection, will open on November 6 in Katonah, New York, functioning as a new home for the renowned trove of contemporary Native art.Building on the private collection's focus on Indigenous and anti-colonial art, Branchline will present rotating exhibitions of the over 800 works by contemporary Native artists in the Gochman Collection and provide residential and studio spaces for artists. Deriving its name from the network of rail lines that connect Katonah to surrounding areas like Manhattan and Upstate New York, Branchline also encompasses the ancestral and historical lineages informing the featured art."We imagine this as a flexible space to not only more broadly share the Collection, but to also create opportunities for varied audiences of artists, scholars, students, families, and our neighbors to spend time together," Laura Phipps, who became the collection's director in March, told Hyperallergic.Jeffrey Gibson's (Mississippi Band of Choctaw and Cherokee) "ACTION NOW ACTION IS ELOQUENCE" (2024) (photo Max Yawney, courtesy Gochman Family Collection)

title: Truman Lowe Listens to the Water
description:
Art Review
								In his first major retrospective, the Hoocąk artist transforms natural materials into fluid sculptures that carry the m
body:
Art Review
								In his first major retrospective, the Hoocąk artist transforms natural materials into fluid sculptures that carry the memory of place, ancestry, and cultural survival.
						
								
																
														
								
						
		
	  		    
        
            Truman Lowe, “Ottawa” (1992), pine, peeled wood saplings (all photos Chinyere Erondu/Hyperallergic)
    
		
				
						WASHINGTON, DC — Hoocąk (Ho-Chunk) artist Truman Lowe’s first major retrospective opens with “Ottawa” (1992), a billowing sculpture of pine and peeled willow saplings that brings together the tributary currents of the rivers that marked the aquatic realms of his childhood. The form undulates with an audacious disregard for the material’s inherent fixed state; each bend, movement, and ripple echoes Lowe’s unwavering ethos that wood is water.Throughout Water’s Edge: The Art of Truman Lowe at the National Museum of the American Indian, Lowe resonates with Toni Morrison’s sentiment that “all water has a perfect memory and is forever trying to get back to where it was.” The works are arranged around four themes of moving water: Landscape and Place, Woodland Structures, Memory, and Shared Knowledge. In Hoocąk culture, the number four holds reverence, history, and the recognition that repetition signifies permanence. This durability appears in multiple works by Lowe, such as “Mimi” (1979), a sculpture composed of four peeled willow branches, four groupings of blue jay feathers, and collections of red beads in sequences of four that cocoon the four strips of leather. Truman Lowe, “Wána (Cascade)" (2002), aluminium
